triples.relationship: later identification and citation of the prophet
triples.rationale: Micah's opening places Michaiah of Morashthi in Hezekiah's reign. Jeremiah identifies Micah the Morathite in that reign and cites the warning found in Micah 3:12. The reign and cited warning support the connection while the supplied name forms remain unchanged.
triples.source_text: The word of the Lord came to Michaiah of Morashthi in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, concerning what he saw about Samaria and Jerusalem.

target_units.text: Micah the Morathite lived in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah and said to all Judah’s people: Thus said the Lord: Zion will be plowed as a field, Jerusalem will become an untrodden place, and the house’s mountain a grove of woodland.

Did Hezekiah and all Judah kill him? Was it not that they feared the Lord and entreated the Lord’s face, and the Lord ceased from the evils He spoke against them? And we have done great evils against our own lives!

triples.relationship: earth summoned before divine testimony and judgment
triples.rationale: Micah summons the peoples and earth to attend to the Lord's testimony from His holy house. The psalm likewise summons the earth, presents God's manifestation from Zion and calls heaven and earth to His judgment.
triples.source_text: Hear words, you peoples! Let the earth and everyone in it attend! The Lord will be among you as a testimony, the Lord from His holy house.

target_units.text: A psalm of Asaph. The God of gods, the Lord, spoke and summoned the earth from the sun’s risings to its settings.
From Zion comes the splendor of His beauty; God will come manifestly,
our God, and He will not keep silent; fire will burn before Him, and around Him is a mighty tempest.
He will summon heaven above and the earth, to judge His people.
Gather His holy ones to Him, those who establish His covenant over sacrifices.
The heavens will announce His righteousness, for God is judge. Diapsalma.

triples.relationship: judgment proceeding from God's dwelling to the earth
triples.rationale: Micah depicts the Lord coming out of His place and descending upon the earth's heights. Isaiah announces the Lord bringing wrath from the holy place upon earth's inhabitants; both move from God's dwelling to judgment on earth.
triples.source_text: For look, the Lord is coming out of His place; He will descend and step upon the heights of the earth,

target_units.text: For behold, the Lord brings wrath from the holy place upon those dwelling on the earth. The earth will uncover its blood and will not cover those killed.

triples.relationship: shaken earth and wax-melting imagery
triples.rationale: Micah's mountains are shaken and its valleys melt like wax before fire. The psalm likewise describes the shaken earth, with mountains melting like wax before the Lord. The shared shaking and wax imagery preserve the different landscape features named as melting.
triples.source_text: and the mountains will be shaken beneath Him, and the valleys will melt like wax before fire and like water flowing downhill.

target_units.text: His lightning flashes shone upon the inhabited world; the earth saw and was shaken.
The mountains melted like wax before the Lord, before the Lord of all the earth.

triples.relationship: Samaria as a focus of Israel's religious offense
triples.rationale: Micah identifies Samaria with Jacob's impiety. Hosea rebukes Samaria's calf, declares that a craftsman made it and it is no god, and speaks of God's anger. Both locate Israel's offense concretely in Samaria.
triples.source_text: All this is because of Jacob’s impiety and the sin of Israel’s house. What is Jacob’s impiety? Is it not Samaria? And what is the sin of Judah’s house? Is it not Jerusalem?

target_units.text: Rub away your calf, Samaria! My anger was provoked against them. How long will they be incapable of being cleansed
in Israel? A craftsman made it, and it is no god, because your calf was leading people astray, Samaria.

triples.relationship: same-book parallel fates of the two capitals
triples.rationale: Samaria is to become a fruit watcher's hut amid agricultural ground. The later warning similarly makes Jerusalem a fruit watcher's hut and Zion a plowed field, linking the two capitals named in the book's opening through parallel ruin imagery.
triples.source_text: I will make Samaria a fruit watcher’s hut in a field and a vineyard plantation. I will pull her stones down into a chasm and uncover her foundations.

target_units.text: Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will be like a fruit watcher’s hut, and the mountain of the house like a forest grove.

triples.relationship: destruction of idolatrous objects
triples.rationale: Micah announces the cutting up of Samaria's carved images and obliteration of her idols. Deuteronomy commands the burning of graven images. The shared connection is destruction of the images; Micah specifically assigns the wages to the fire.
triples.source_text: They will cut up all her carved images and burn all her wages in fire, and I will consign all her idols to obliteration. For she gathered from prostitution wages and amassed from prostitution wages.

target_units.text: You shall burn the graven images of their gods with fire. You shall not covet the silver or gold upon them, nor take it unto yourself, lest you stumble thereby; for it is an abomination unto the Lord your God.

triples.relationship: lament associated with sirens
triples.rationale: Micah compares the city's lament with dragons and daughters of sirens. Job calls himself a brother to sirens while describing crying out and song becoming weeping. Both associate lament with sirens, preserving their differing companion animal names.
triples.source_text: Because of this she will lament and mourn; she will go barefoot and naked. She will make lamentation like dragons and mourning like daughters of sirens.

target_units.text: I have gone about groaning without a muzzle; I have stood in an assembly, crying out.
I have become a brother to sirens and a companion to ostriches.
My skin has darkened greatly, and my bones are scorched from heat.
My lyre became an expression of my suffering, and my song became weeping for me.”

triples.relationship: narrative counterpart to a threat reaching Jerusalem
triples.rationale: Micah says the blow reaches Judah and Jerusalem. Kings narrates the Assyrian capture of Judah's fortified cities and a great force sent onward to Jerusalem. The connection concerns that advance into Judah toward Jerusalem, without equating every detail of the oracle with the campaign.
triples.source_text: For her blow has prevailed; it came as far as Judah and touched the gate of My people, as far as Jerusalem.

target_units.text: In King Hezekiah’s fourteenth year, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians went up against Judah’s fortified cities and captured them.

Hezekiah king of Judah sent messengers to the king of the Assyrians at Lachish: ‘I have sinned. Withdraw from me; whatever you impose on me, I will bear.’ The king of the Assyrians imposed on Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.
Hezekiah gave all the silver found in the Lord’s house and in the treasuries of the king’s house.
At that time Hezekiah cut apart the doors of the Lord’s sanctuary and the fixed supports which Hezekiah king of Judah had gilded, and gave them to the king of the Assyrians.

The king of the Assyrians sent Tharthan, Raphis, and Rhapsakes from Lachish to King Hezekiah against Jerusalem with a great force. They went up, came to Jerusalem, and stood at the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road of the Fuller’s Field.

triples.relationship: Gath and rejoicing over Israel's calamity
triples.rationale: Micah tells those in Gath not to magnify themselves in the midst of the lament. David likewise forbids reporting Israel's defeat in Gath lest foreign daughters rejoice. Both address Gath's possible exultation over Israel's misfortune.
triples.source_text: You in Gath, do not magnify yourselves! You in Akim, do not rebuild from a house for laughter; sprinkle yourselves with earth in keeping with your laughter.

target_units.text: Do not report it in Gath, and do not proclaim good news in Ashkelon’s exits, lest the daughters of the foreigners rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.

triples.relationship: parallel divine judgment against Jerusalem
triples.rationale: Micah attributes the calamities at Jerusalem's gates to the Lord. Ezekiel explicitly identifies Jerusalem and declares that the Lord is against her and will execute judgment within her because His ordinances were rejected.
triples.source_text: Who began good things for the woman dwelling in pains? For calamities came down from the Lord upon Jerusalem’s gates,

target_units.text: ‘Thus says the Lord: This is Jerusalem. I have placed her amid the nations, and the lands around her.
And you will speak My ordinances to the lawless one among the nations, and My laws among the lands around her; for they rejected My ordinances and did not walk in My laws.

Therefore thus says the Lord: Because your impulse comes from the nations around you, and you have not walked in My laws or performed My ordinances—nor have you even acted according to the ordinances of the nations around you—
therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I am against you, and I will execute judgment in your midst before the nations,

triples.relationship: military connection between Lachish and Jerusalem
triples.rationale: Micah addresses Lachish amid the noise of chariots and horsemen and relates her to Zion's trouble. Kings records an Assyrian force sent from Lachish against Jerusalem. Both passages connect the two cities in a military setting, without making the historical report explain every charge against Lachish.
triples.source_text: the noise of chariots and horsemen. Inhabitant of Lachish, she is a leader of sin to the daughter of Zion, for Israel’s impieties were found in you.

target_units.text: The king of the Assyrians sent Tharthan, Raphis, and Rhapsakes from Lachish to King Hezekiah against Jerusalem with a great force. They went up, came to Jerusalem, and stood at the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road of the Fuller’s Field.

triples.relationship: hair cutting and mourning for loved ones
triples.rationale: Micah commands shaving and shearing in mourning for children taken captive. Amos likewise joins baldness on every head with lamentation and mourning for a beloved one. The shared mourning signs are retained without changing Micah's separate widowhood-and-eagle wording.
triples.source_text: Shave yourself and shear your hair for your delicate children. Enlarge your widowhood like an eagle, for they have been taken captive away from you.

target_units.text: I will turn your festivals to mourning and all your songs to lamentation. I will put sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head; I will make him like mourning for a beloved one, and those with him like a day of pain.

triples.relationship: evil planned upon a bed
triples.rationale: Micah describes wrongdoers planning evil on their beds before carrying it out. The psalm likewise depicts the lawless person devising lawlessness upon his bed and refusing the good way.
triples.source_text: They became people planning troubles and working evil on their beds, and at daybreak they carried them out, because they did not raise their hands to God.

target_units.text: The lawless person speaks within himself of sinning; there is no fear of God before his eyes.
For he acted deceitfully in his sight, as to finding his lawlessness and hating it.
The words of his mouth are lawlessness and deceit; he was unwilling to understand so as to do good.
He devised lawlessness upon his bed; he stood by every way that was not good, and he was not offended by wickedness.

triples.relationship: parallel condemnation of land seizure
triples.rationale: Micah condemns coveting fields and plundering a person, house and inheritance. Isaiah likewise condemns joining house to house and field to field in order to take from a neighbor.
triples.source_text: They coveted fields and plundered orphans, oppressed houses and plundered a man and his house, a man and his inheritance.

target_units.text: Woe to those joining house to house and bringing field beside field, so that they may take something from their neighbor! Surely you will not dwell alone upon the earth?

triples.relationship: narrative example of seized inheritance
triples.rationale: Micah condemns taking a person's field and inheritance. Kings records Ahab going to possess Naboth's vineyard after Naboth's death, following the refusal to surrender his ancestral inheritance in the surrounding account.
triples.source_text: They coveted fields and plundered orphans, oppressed houses and plundered a man and his house, a man and his inheritance.

target_units.text: When Jezebel heard, she said to Ahab, “Rise, take possession of Naboth the Jezreelite’s vineyard, which he did not give you for silver. Naboth is no longer alive; he is dead.”
When Ahab heard that Naboth the Jezreelite was dead, he tore his garments and put on sackcloth. After this, Ahab rose and went down to Naboth the Jezreelite’s vineyard to take possession of it.

triples.relationship: parallel announcement of planned calamity
triples.rationale: The Lord declares that He is planning calamities against the offending tribe. Jeremiah similarly announces the Lord's shaping evils and devising a design against Judah and Jerusalem, alongside a call to turn from evil practices.
triples.source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: “Look, I am planning calamities against this tribe, from which you will certainly not lift your necks, and you will certainly not suddenly walk upright, for it is an evil time.

target_units.text: And now say to Judah’s men and those dwelling in Jerusalem: Behold, I am shaping evils against you and devising a design against you. Let each turn from his evil way now, and make your practices better.

triples.relationship: shared loss through division of the people's land
triples.rationale: Micah's lament says the people's portion was measured and their fields divided. Joel announces judgment over the nations concerning Israel's scattering and the division of the Lord's land. Both describe dispossession through division of the land.
triples.source_text: On that day a parable will be taken up against you, and a lament will be sung in melody, saying: ‘We have suffered grievous misery! The portion of My people was measured with a cord, and there was no one to prevent him from turning away; our fields were divided.’

target_units.text: I will gather all the nations and bring them down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. There I will enter into judgment with them over My people and My inheritance Israel, who were scattered among the nations; and they divided up My land

triples.relationship: loss contrasted with inheritance allotted by lot
triples.rationale: Micah threatens the loss of anyone casting a measuring cord by lot in the Lord's assembly. Joshua's account surveys the land into portions and casts a lot before the Lord, providing the positive allotment practice with which Micah's exclusion contrasts.
triples.source_text: Therefore you will have no one casting a measuring cord by lot in the assembly of the Lord.

target_units.text: The men rose and went. Joshua commanded the men going to survey the land, saying, “Go and survey the land and return to me. Here at Shiloh I will bring out a lot for you before the Lord.”
They went, surveyed the land, saw it, and wrote it by its cities in seven portions in a scroll, which they brought to Joshua.
Joshua cast a lot for them at Shiloh before the Lord.

triples.relationship: provoking God's Spirit
triples.rationale: Micah cites the claim that Jacob's house provoked the Lord's Spirit. Isaiah describes the people disobeying and provoking His holy spirit, followed by the Lord turning against them. The connection concerns the stated provocation, not an imported claim that God's patience is short.
triples.source_text: The one who says, ‘Jacob’s house has provoked the Lord’s Spirit’: Are these his practices? Are not his words good with him, and have they walked uprightly?

target_units.text: But they disobeyed and provoked His holy spirit. He turned toward hostility against them and Himself fought them.

triples.relationship: same-book imagery of flaying the people
triples.rationale: Micah 2 describes hostility through the image of flaying skin. Chapter 3 develops the charge against leaders with skins stripped from the people and their flesh treated as meat, repeating the book's bodily imagery of abuse.
triples.source_text: And formerly My people stood opposed in enmity; facing his peace, they flayed his skin to take away hope—a shattering of war.

target_units.text: you who hate good things and seek evil things, who snatch their skins from them and their flesh from their bones?”
Just as they ate the flesh of My people, flayed their skins from their bones, crushed their bones and divided them into pieces like flesh for a cauldron and meat for a cooking pot,

triples.relationship: luxury followed by captivity
triples.rationale: Micah says the people's leaders will be expelled from luxurious houses because of their practices. Amos likewise describes powerful people reclining on ivory beds and enjoying costly food and perfume, then announces captivity.
triples.source_text: Therefore the leaders of My people will be cast out of their luxurious houses; because of their evil practices they were expelled. Draw near to everlasting mountains!

target_units.text: sleeping upon ivory beds and indulging upon your couches, eating young goats from the flocks and milk-fed calves from the herds,
clapping to the sound of instruments; they reckoned them as lasting, not passing away,
drinking strained wine and anointing yourselves with the finest perfumes, yet suffering nothing over Joseph’s shattering.
Therefore now they will be captives from the foremost of the powerful, and horses’ neighing will be removed from Ephraim.

triples.relationship: uncleanness and loss of a place to remain
triples.rationale: Micah commands departure because uncleanness has made the place no resting place. Leviticus connects defilement of the land with the Lord driving out its inhabitants and warns Israel against the same defilement.
triples.source_text: Rise and go, for this is no resting place for you because of uncleanness. You were corrupted with corruption,

target_units.text: Do not defile yourselves in any of these things; for in all these things the nations whom I drive out before your face were defiled,
and the land became defiled, and I repaid them for wrongdoing because of it, and the land became indignant with those settled upon it.
And you shall keep all My statutes and all My commands, and do none of these abominations, neither the native nor the resident foreigner who has joined himself among you—
for the people of the land who were before you did all these abominations, and the land became defiled—
so that the land is not indignant with you when you defile it, as it was indignant with the nations before you.

triples.relationship: shared pursuit-without-a-pursuer language
triples.rationale: Micah describes being pursued with no one pursuing. Leviticus' covenant sanctions include fleeing when no one pursues, alongside defeat before enemies. The paradoxical pursuit language is the specific connection.
triples.source_text: you were pursued with no one pursuing. A spirit established falsehood; it dripped to you into wine and strong drink. And it will be from the drop of this people:

target_units.text: And I will set My face against you, and you shall fall before your enemies. Those who hate you shall pursue you, and you shall flee when no one pursues you.

triples.relationship: Israel's gathering portrayed as a flock
triples.rationale: Micah promises to gather Israel's remaining ones, compares them with sheep in affliction and a flock within its resting place, and says they will leap out from among people. Ezekiel likewise uses flock language for gathering from countries, then explicitly promises pasture and rest.
triples.source_text: Jacob will surely be gathered with everyone. I will surely receive Israel’s remaining ones; I will put their turning back together. Like sheep in affliction, like a flock within their resting place, they will leap out from among people.

target_units.text: I will bring them out from the nations, gather them from the countries and bring them into their own land. I will feed them upon Israel’s mountains, in the ravines and in every dwelling place of the land.
I will feed them in good pasture, and their folds will be upon Israel’s high mountain. There they will lie down, there rest in good delight, and graze in rich pasture upon Israel’s mountains.
I Myself will feed My sheep and give them rest, and they will know that I am the Lord. Thus says the Lord, the Lord:

triples.relationship: shared flock leadership through an opening
triples.rationale: Micah's gathered flock passes through a gate with its king before it and the Lord leading. John describes the opened sheepfold, the shepherd leading his sheep out and going before them. The connection is the shared leadership image, not a claim that the passages narrate the same event.
triples.source_text: Through the breach before them they broke through, passed a gate and went out through it. Their king went out before them, and the Lord will lead them.”

target_units.text: To him the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.
When he has brought all his own out, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.

triples.relationship: leaders' responsibility for justice
triples.rationale: Micah asks Israel's authorities whether they ought to know justice. Deuteronomy directs appointed judges and officers to judge the people with righteous judgment, supplying the explicit responsibility challenged by the question.
triples.source_text: He will say: “Hear these things now, authorities of Jacob’s house and remaining ones of Israel’s house! Is it not for you to know justice,

target_units.text: You shall appoint judges and recording officers for yourself in all your cities which the Lord your God gives you, according to your tribes; and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment.

triples.relationship: opposition between corrupt preferences and the call to good
triples.rationale: Micah accuses leaders of hating good and seeking evil. Amos calls for seeking good rather than evil and restoring judgment, directly opposing the preferences Micah condemns.
triples.source_text: you who hate good things and seek evil things, who snatch their skins from them and their flesh from their bones?”

target_units.text: Seek the good and not the evil, so that you may live; then the Lord God Almighty will be with you, just as you said,
“We have hated evil things and loved good things.” Restore judgment at the gates, so that the Lord God Almighty may have mercy on Joseph’s remaining ones.

triples.relationship: shared imagery of devouring the people
triples.rationale: Micah describes the people's flesh treated as meat for a cooking pot. The psalm similarly accuses lawless people of devouring the people like a meal of bread. Both use eating imagery to portray abuse of the people.
triples.source_text: Just as they ate the flesh of My people, flayed their skins from their bones, crushed their bones and divided them into pieces like flesh for a cauldron and meat for a cooking pot,

target_units.text: Will all those who practice lawlessness not know? Those who devour my people as a meal of bread did not call upon the Lord.

triples.relationship: violence followed by rejected prayer
triples.rationale: Micah says the Lord will not hear the cry of those who acted wickedly against the people and will turn His face away. Isaiah likewise says He will turn His eyes away and refuse multiplied supplications because their hands are full of blood.
triples.source_text: so they will cry to the Lord, but He will not listen to them. He will turn His face away from them at that time, because they acted wickedly in their practices against them.

target_units.text: Whenever you stretch your hands toward Me, I will turn My eyes away from you. Even if you multiply supplication, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood.

triples.relationship: corrupt prophetic pronouncements tied to food
triples.rationale: Micah's misleading prophets proclaim peace when their mouths are supplied and raise war when they are not. Ezekiel condemns profaning God through vain pronouncements for barley and scraps of bread; both connect deceptive prophetic activity with food received.
triples.source_text: Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead My people astray, who bite with their teeth and proclaim peace to him; but when nothing was put into their mouths, they raised war against him:

target_units.text: They were profaning Me among My people for a handful of barley and scraps of bread, putting to death lives that ought not die and preserving lives that ought not live, as you uttered things to a people listening to vain pronouncements.

triples.relationship: shared judgment imagery of lost daylight
triples.rationale: Micah announces night in place of vision and sunset over the prophets. Amos similarly announces the sun setting at midday and light becoming dark during daytime. Micah applies the darkness specifically to the prophets' loss of vision.
triples.source_text: “Therefore you will have night instead of vision and darkness instead of divination; the sun will set upon the prophets, and the day will darken over them.

target_units.text: “On that day,” says the Lord God, “the sun will set at midday, and the light will grow dark upon the earth in daytime.

triples.relationship: prophets ashamed of their visions
triples.rationale: Micah announces shame for dream-seers and mockery for diviners. Zechariah likewise says prophets will be ashamed because of their visions when they prophesy.
triples.source_text: Those seeing dreams will be ashamed and the diviners mocked; all of them will speak against them, because there will be no one listening to them,

target_units.text: On that day the prophets will be ashamed, each because of his vision when he prophesies; they will wear a hairy skin because they lied.

triples.relationship: commission to declare Jacob's sins
triples.rationale: Micah links strength in the Lord's Spirit with declaring Jacob's impieties and Israel's sins. Isaiah likewise commands a strong public proclamation of the people's sins and Jacob's lawless acts.
triples.source_text: unless I fill up strength in the Spirit of the Lord and of judgment and might, to declare to Jacob his impieties and to Israel his sins.”

target_units.text: “Shout with strength and do not spare! Raise your voice like a trumpet and announce My people’s sins to them, and Jacob’s house their lawless acts.

triples.relationship: perverted justice opposed to the legal requirement
triples.rationale: Micah charges leaders with abhorring justice and twisting what is straight. Deuteronomy forbids perverting judgment and commands pursuit of what is just, directly opposing that conduct.
triples.source_text: Hear these things now, leaders of Jacob’s house and remaining ones of Israel’s house, who abhor justice and twist all straight things,

target_units.text: They shall not pervert judgment, neither shall they show partiality, nor take a bribe; for bribes blind the eyes of the wise, and overthrow the words of the righteous.
You shall pursue justly that which is just, that you may live, and enter and inherit the land which the Lord your God gives you.

triples.relationship: parallel condemnation of building with bloodshed
triples.rationale: Micah condemns building Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with injustices. Habakkuk pronounces woe on building and preparing a city with bloodshed and injustices, repeating the distinctive city-building accusation.
triples.source_text: you who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with injustices!

target_units.text: Woe to the one building a city with bloodshed and preparing a city with injustices!

triples.relationship: judicial payment opposed to the ban on bribes
triples.rationale: Micah accuses Jerusalem's leaders of judging for gifts. Deuteronomy explicitly forbids judges taking a bribe because it blinds the wise and overturns righteous words.
triples.source_text: Her leaders judged with gifts, her priests answered for wages and her prophets divined for silver; yet they relied upon the Lord, saying, “Is not the Lord among us? Calamities will certainly not come upon us.”

target_units.text: They shall not pervert judgment, neither shall they show partiality, nor take a bribe; for bribes blind the eyes of the wise, and overthrow the words of the righteous.

triples.relationship: explicit later citation of Micah's warning
triples.rationale: Jeremiah explicitly attributes to Micah the warning that Zion will be plowed as a field and the house's mountain become woodland. Those clauses correspond to this verse; Jeremiah's description of Jerusalem as an untrodden place is preserved alongside Micah's fruit watcher's hut wording.
triples.source_text: Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will be like a fruit watcher’s hut, and the mountain of the house like a forest grove.

target_units.text: Micah the Morathite lived in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah and said to all Judah’s people: Thus said the Lord: Zion will be plowed as a field, Jerusalem will become an untrodden place, and the house’s mountain a grove of woodland.

Did Hezekiah and all Judah kill him? Was it not that they feared the Lord and entreated the Lord’s face, and the Lord ceased from the evils He spoke against them? And we have done great evils against our own lives!

triples.relationship: parallel oracle of the elevated Lord's mountain
triples.rationale: Both passages locate the vision in the last days, raise the Lord's mountain above surrounding heights and describe peoples or nations coming toward it.
triples.source_text: In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, established upon the mountain summits and raised above the hills, and peoples will hurry toward it.

target_units.text: In the last days the Lord’s mountain and God’s house will be clearly visible on the summits of the mountains and be raised above the hills; all the nations will come to it,

triples.relationship: parallel invitation to learn at Zion
triples.rationale: Both passages have nations invite one another to the Lord's mountain and Jacob's God's house, to learn His way and walk in it. Both end with law going from Zion and the Lord's word from Jerusalem.
triples.source_text: Many nations will go and say, “Come, let us go up to the Lord’s mountain and to the house of Jacob’s God. They will show us His way, and we will walk in His paths.” For law will go out from Zion, and the Lord’s word from Jerusalem.

target_units.text: and many nations will go and say, “Come, let us go up to the Lord’s mountain and to the house of Jacob’s God. He will announce His way to us, and we will walk in it.” For law will go out from Zion, and the Lord’s word from Jerusalem.

triples.relationship: parallel transformation of weapons into tools
triples.rationale: Both describe divine judgment among peoples followed by swords becoming plows and spears becoming sickles. Each concludes with nations no longer taking up war or learning to wage it.
triples.source_text: He will judge between many peoples and reprove strong nations as far as a distant land. They will cut their swords into plows and their spears into sickles. Nation will certainly no longer raise sword against nation, nor will they learn to wage war anymore.

target_units.text: He will judge between the nations and reprove a numerous people. They will beat their swords into plows and their spears into sickles. Nation will no longer take sword against nation, and they will certainly no longer learn to wage war.

triples.relationship: contrasting prophetic uses of weapons and farming tools
triples.rationale: Micah describes weapons remade into farming tools as war ends. Joel reverses that direction, ordering farming tools made into weapons while gathering nations for judgment. The same implements serve contrasting scenes in their respective oracles.
triples.source_text: He will judge between many peoples and reprove strong nations as far as a distant land. They will cut their swords into plows and their spears into sickles. Nation will certainly no longer raise sword against nation, nor will they learn to wage war anymore.

target_units.text: Beat your plows into swords and your sickles into lances; let the powerless say, “I am strong!”
Assemble and enter, all surrounding nations, and gather there! Let the meek become a fighter!
Let all the nations be roused and come up to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, because there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.

triples.relationship: parallel vine-and-fig-tree peace imagery
triples.rationale: Micah promises rest beneath each person's vine and fig tree without fear. Zechariah likewise pictures neighbors invited beneath a vine and fig tree in the promised day.
triples.source_text: Each will rest beneath his vine and each beneath his fig tree, and there will be no one causing fear, because the mouth of the Lord Almighty has spoken these things.

target_units.text: On that day, says the Lord Almighty, each of you will invite his neighbor beneath a vine and beneath a fig tree.”

triples.relationship: shared declaration of allegiance to the Lord
triples.rationale: Micah contrasts the peoples' own ways with the community's lasting walk in the Lord's name. Joshua similarly contrasts available objects of service with his household's declared service of the Lord.
triples.source_text: For all the peoples will walk, each his own way, but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God forever and beyond.

target_units.text: But if it does not please you to serve the Lord, choose for yourselves today whom you will serve: the gods of your fathers beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But I and my house will serve the Lord, for He is holy.”

triples.relationship: parallel gathering of the crushed and rejected
triples.rationale: Micah promises to gather the crushed and receive the expelled. Zephaniah likewise promises gathering of the crushed and saving and receiving the oppressed and rejected.
triples.source_text: “On that day,” says the Lord, “I will gather the crushed one, receive the expelled one and those I rejected.

target_units.text: I will gather the crushed. Alas! Who took up reproach against her?
Look, I am acting within you for your sake at that time, says the Lord. I will save the oppressed and the rejected; I will receive them and make them a boast and renowned throughout the earth.

triples.relationship: the Lord's kingship associated with Mount Zion
triples.rationale: Micah promises that the Lord will reign over the restored people on Mount Zion. Obadiah likewise joins people ascending from Mount Zion with the declaration that the kingdom will be the Lord's.
triples.source_text: I will make the crushed one a remnant and the rejected one a strong nation. The Lord will reign over them on Mount Zion from now and forever.

target_units.text: And men who have been saved shall ascend from Mount Zion to execute judgment upon the mountain of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the Lord’s.

triples.relationship: Zion's distress compared to labor pains
triples.rationale: Micah asks why Zion has been seized with pains like a woman giving birth. Jeremiah likewise describes the daughter of Zion's voice and groaning as those of a woman in labor amid calamity.
triples.source_text: And now why have you experienced calamities? Did you have no king? Has your counsel perished, that birth pains have seized you like a woman giving birth?

target_units.text: For I heard a voice like a woman in labor, your groaning like one giving birth for the first time, the voice of the daughter of Zion. She will grow faint and let her hands fall: Woe to me, because my soul fails over those killed!

triples.relationship: rescue from Babylon
triples.rationale: Micah announces that Zion will reach Babylon and that the Lord will redeem her there from enemies. Isaiah calls the people to leave Babylon and proclaim that the Lord rescued His servant Jacob.
triples.source_text: Labor in birth, be courageous and draw near, daughter of Zion, like a woman giving birth! For now you will go out from the city, camp in the plain and come as far as Babylon. From there He will rescue you, and from there the Lord your God will redeem you from your enemies’ hand.

target_units.text: Leave Babylon, fleeing from the Chaldeans. Announce a voice of rejoicing, and let this be heard; proclaim it to the earth’s extremity. Say, “The Lord rescued His slave Jacob.”

triples.relationship: hostile rejoicing over Judah's distress
triples.rationale: Micah describes gathered nations declaring that they will rejoice over Zion. Obadiah explicitly forbids rejoicing and boasting over Judah's destruction and affliction, condemning the response Micah attributes to the hostile nations.
triples.source_text: Now many nations have gathered against you, saying, “We will rejoice over her, and our eyes will look upon Zion!”

target_units.text: Do not look on your brother’s day, on the day of strangers; do not rejoice over the sons of Judah on the day of their destruction; do not speak boastfully on the day of affliction.

triples.relationship: gathered nations compared to an agricultural judgment
triples.rationale: Micah says the nations have been gathered like sheaves on a threshing floor despite not understanding God's counsel. Joel likewise gathers nations for judgment and depicts a ready vintage and full winepress. The agricultural forms differ, but both portray their gathering as preparation for judgment.
triples.source_text: But they did not know the Lord’s thought or understand His counsel, for He gathered them like sheaves of a threshing floor.

target_units.text: Assemble and enter, all surrounding nations, and gather there! Let the meek become a fighter!
Let all the nations be roused and come up to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, because there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.
Send out sickles, because the vintage is at hand! Enter and tread, because the winepress is full; the vats overflow, because their evils have multiplied.

triples.relationship: Israel equipped for threshing imagery of victory
triples.rationale: Micah equips Zion with iron horns and bronze hooves to thresh and grind peoples. Isaiah makes Jacob like saw-toothed threshing wagon wheels that grind mountains and hills into dust. Both portray the people as divinely equipped threshing instruments.
triples.source_text: Rise and thresh them, daughter of Zion, for I will make your horns iron and your hooves bronze. With them you will melt down nations and grind many peoples fine; you will dedicate their multitude to the Lord and their strength to the Lord of all the earth.

target_units.text: Jacob, little Israel. I helped you,’ says God who redeems you, Israel.
Behold, I made you like new, saw-toothed wagon wheels for threshing. You will thresh mountains, grind hills fine, and make them like dust.
You will winnow, and wind will take them and a storm scatter them. But you will rejoice among Israel’s holy ones. And they will exult—

triples.relationship: shared image of humiliating blows to the cheeks
triples.rationale: Micah announces that Israel's tribes will be struck on the cheek with a rod. Isaiah's speaker gives his cheeks to slaps and faces shameful spitting. The connection is the depicted facial humiliation; the passages' subjects are preserved as distinct.
triples.source_text: Now the daughter of Ephraim will be fenced in with a barrier; he has set a constraint upon us. With a rod they will strike Israel’s tribes on the cheek.

target_units.text: I have given my back to scourges and my cheeks to slaps. I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting.

triples.relationship: explicit later use of the Bethlehem ruler oracle
triples.rationale: Micah announces a ruler for Israel coming from Bethlehem. Matthew explicitly introduces a prophetic text naming Bethlehem as the ruler's birthplace in response to the question about the Christ. Matthew's by-no-means-least formulation remains distinct from Micah's smallness wording.
triples.source_text: And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are small to be among Judah’s thousands; from you one will come out for Me to be a ruler in Israel, and his goings out are from the beginning, from days of old.

target_units.text: He gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people and asked them where the Christ was to be born.
They told him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for this is what has been written through the prophet:
‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for out of you will come a ruler who will shepherd My people Israel.’”

triples.relationship: childbirth associated with a people's restoration
triples.rationale: Micah connects the woman's giving birth with the remaining brothers' return to Israel. Isaiah connects Zion giving birth to her children with the birth of a nation. The shared childbirth-and-people imagery does not identify Micah's unnamed woman with a particular individual.
triples.source_text: Therefore he will give them up until the time of the woman giving birth, when she gives birth; then the remaining ones of their brothers will return to the sons of Israel.

target_units.text: Before the woman in labor gave birth, before the pain of labor came, she escaped and bore a male.
Who heard such a thing, and who has seen anything like it? Did a land labor in one day, or was a nation born all at once? For Zion labored and bore her children.
‘But I gave this expectation, and you did not remember Me,’ said the Lord. ‘Behold, did I not make the woman who gives birth and the barren woman?’ said God.

triples.relationship: parallel shepherd-ruler promises
triples.rationale: Micah's promised ruler will shepherd his flock in the Lord's strength. Ezekiel likewise promises one shepherd, God's servant David, and calls him a ruler among the people, joining shepherding with rule under the Lord.
triples.source_text: He will stand, see and shepherd his flock in the Lord’s strength, and they will exist in the glory of the name of the Lord their God; for now he will be magnified to the ends of the earth.

target_units.text: I will raise up one shepherd over them, My servant David, and he will shepherd them and be their shepherd.
I, the Lord, will be their God, and David a ruler among them. I, the Lord, have spoken.

triples.relationship: parallel response to Assyrian intrusion
triples.rationale: Micah describes an Assyrian entering the land and a response raised against him. Isaiah promises destruction of the Assyrians from the Lord's land and mountains. Both address Assyrian intrusion and its reversal; Micah's seven shepherds and eight bites wording is left intact.
triples.source_text: This will be peace: when an Assyrian comes upon your land and steps upon your country, seven shepherds and eight bites of people will rise against him.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord Sabaoth: “As I said, so it will be, and as I counseled, so it will endure,
to destroy the Assyrians from My land and from My mountains. They will become a trampling place; their yoke will be removed from them, and their glory removed from the shoulders.”

triples.relationship: parallel deliverance from Assyria's power
triples.rationale: Micah promises rescue from Assour when he crosses the land's borders. Isaiah similarly announces removal of the Assyrians from the land and removal of their yoke.
triples.source_text: They will shepherd Assour with the sword and Nebrod’s land in its ditch. He will rescue from Assour when he comes upon your land and steps upon your borders.

target_units.text: to destroy the Assyrians from My land and from My mountains. They will become a trampling place; their yoke will be removed from them, and their glory removed from the shoulders.”

triples.relationship: dew imagery connected with Israel and the Lord
triples.rationale: Micah compares Jacob's remnant among the peoples with dew falling from the Lord. Hosea promises that the Lord will be like dew to Israel. Both connect Israel and dew with the Lord, while assigning the image differently.
triples.source_text: Jacob’s remnant will be among the nations, amid many peoples, like dew falling from the Lord and like lambs upon couch grass, so that no one may be gathered or stand among the sons of humankind.

target_units.text: I will be like dew to Israel; he will blossom like a lily and put down his roots like Lebanon.

triples.relationship: shared lion imagery with no rescuer
triples.rationale: Micah depicts the remnant as a lion seizing among flocks with no one to deliver. Hosea likewise uses a lion comparison and seizure with no one to rescue. Micah applies the image to the remnant; Hosea applies it to the Lord's judgment against Judah.
triples.source_text: Jacob’s remnant will be among the nations, amid many peoples, like a lion among beasts in the forest and like a young lion among flocks of sheep, which passes through, separates and seizes, with no one to deliver.

target_units.text: For I am like a panther to Ephraim and like a lion to Judah’s house. I seize and will go away and take, and there will be no one to rescue.

triples.relationship: hands over enemies as victory imagery
triples.rationale: Micah promises the hand raised over afflicting enemies. Jacob's blessing of Judah likewise places his hands upon his enemies' backs, using the position of the hand to express victory over opponents.
triples.source_text: Your hand will be raised above those afflicting you, and all your enemies will be destroyed.

target_units.text: “Judah, may your brothers praise you; your hands shall be upon the backs of your enemies, and your father’s sons shall bow down to you.

triples.relationship: parallel removal of horses and chariots
triples.rationale: Micah announces destruction of the people's horses and chariots. Zechariah likewise announces the destruction of chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, placing that removal beside peace and the coming king's rule.
triples.source_text: “On that day,” says the Lord, “I will destroy your horses from your midst and destroy your chariots,

target_units.text: He will destroy chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem; the battle bow will be destroyed, and abundance and peace from the nations. He will rule waters as far as the sea and the earth’s river outlets.

triples.relationship: judgment on fortified cities
triples.rationale: Micah promises to destroy cities and remove strongholds. Hosea specifically condemns Judah's multiplication of walled cities and announces fire that will devour their foundations.
triples.source_text: and I will destroy the cities of your land and remove all your strongholds.

target_units.text: Israel forgot his Maker, and they built sacred precincts; Judah multiplied walled cities. I will send fire into his cities, and it will devour their foundations.

triples.relationship: removal of forbidden sorcery and divination
triples.rationale: Micah announces removal of sorceries and utterers of oracles. Deuteronomy forbids sorcery, divination and related practices among Israel and contrasts the nations' reliance on them with the Lord's instruction.
triples.source_text: I will remove your sorceries from your hands, and there will be no utterers of oracles among you.

target_units.text: There shall not be found among you one who purifies his son or his daughter by fire, or practises divination, or interprets spoken omens, or observes auguries, or works sorcery,
or chants spells, or is a medium, or observes portents, or inquires of the dead.
For everyone who does these things is an abomination unto the Lord your God; for because of these abominations the Lord shall destroy them from before you.
You shall be perfect before the Lord your God.
For these nations whose possession you inherit hearken unto omens and divinations; but the Lord your God has not granted you so to do.

triples.relationship: parallel destruction of images and pillars
triples.rationale: Micah promises destruction of carved images and pillars and an end to bowing to handmade works. Deuteronomy commands the breaking of pillars and burning of graven images, sharing the elimination of these objects of worship.
triples.source_text: I will destroy your carved images and pillars from your midst, and you will certainly no longer bow down to the works of your hands.

target_units.text: And you shall pull down their altars, and break their pillars, and cut down their sacred groves, and burn the graven images of their gods with fire; and their name shall perish from that place.

triples.relationship: parallel cutting down of sacred groves
triples.rationale: Micah promises to cut down the groves from the people's midst. Deuteronomy specifically commands cutting down sacred groves along with destroying other objects of foreign worship.
triples.source_text: I will cut down your groves from your midst and obliterate your cities.

target_units.text: And you shall pull down their altars, and break their pillars, and cut down their sacred groves, and burn the graven images of their gods with fire; and their name shall perish from that place.

triples.relationship: parallel wrath against nations
triples.rationale: Micah announces vengeance in anger and wrath among disobedient nations. Isaiah summons nations to hear that the Lord's wrath and anger are against them for destruction, matching the announced agent, recipients and punitive anger.
triples.source_text: I will execute vengeance in anger and wrath among the nations because they did not obey.”

target_units.text: Draw near, nations, and hear, rulers! Let the earth and those in it hear, the inhabited world and the people in it!
For the Lord’s wrath is against all nations, and anger against their number, to destroy them and hand them over to slaughter.

triples.relationship: creation summoned to hear the divine case
triples.rationale: Micah calls for the mountains and hills to hear the word in the setting of judgment. Moses likewise calls heaven and earth to hear his words, using creation as the audience to a declaration concerning God and His people.
triples.source_text: Hear now the word of the Lord. The Lord said: “Rise, enter into judgment before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice.”

target_units.text: Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth.

triples.relationship: creation as witness to God's judgment of His people
triples.rationale: Micah calls the hills, ravines and earth's foundations to hear the Lord's case with Israel. The psalm likewise summons heaven and earth to God's judgment of His covenant people and declares God the judge.
triples.source_text: Hear, hills, the Lord’s judgment, and you ravines, foundations of the earth! For the Lord has a case against His people, and He will argue it with Israel.

target_units.text: He will summon heaven above and the earth, to judge His people.
Gather His holy ones to Him, those who establish His covenant over sacrifices.
The heavens will announce His righteousness, for God is judge. Diapsalma.

triples.relationship: parallel divine question about an alleged offense
triples.rationale: The Lord asks His people what He has done to grieve or trouble them. Jeremiah similarly asks what offense their fathers found in Him that led them away, framing the people's departure against God's challenge to name His wrongdoing.
triples.source_text: “My people, what have I done to you? How have I grieved you, or how have I troubled you? Answer Me!

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: What offense did your fathers find in Me, that they withdrew far from Me, followed futile things and became futile?

triples.relationship: explicit recollection of deliverance from slavery
triples.rationale: Micah recalls the Lord bringing Israel from Egypt and redeeming them from the house of slavery. Exodus uses that same Egypt-and-house-of-bondage description in the Lord's declaration introducing the commandments.
triples.source_text: For I brought you up from Egypt’s land and redeemed you from the house of slavery. I sent Moses, Aaron and Miriam before you.

target_units.text: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.

triples.relationship: explicit recollection of Balak and Balaam
triples.rationale: Micah commands remembrance of Balak's plan and Balaam's answer. Numbers records Balak summoning Balaam to curse Jacob, Balaam's refusal to curse those God does not curse, and Balak's complaint that a blessing was given instead.
triples.source_text: My people, remember what Balak king of Moab planned against you and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from the rushes to Galgal, so that the Lord’s righteousness may be known.”

target_units.text: And God's Spirit came upon him, and he took up his parable and said: Balak summoned me from Mesopotamia, the king of Moab from the eastern mountains: Come, curse Jacob for me; come, call down a curse on Israel for me.
Why should I curse whom the Lord does not curse? Why should I call down a curse on whom God does not curse?
From the tops of mountains I shall see them, and from the hills I shall observe them. Behold, a people who will dwell alone, not counted among the nations.
Who has measured Jacob’s seed exactly, and who will count Israel's clans? May my soul die among righteous souls, and may my seed be like their seed!
And Balak said to Balaam: What have you done to me? I summoned you to curse my enemies, and look, you have pronounced a blessing!
And Balaam said to Balak: Must I not take care to speak what God puts in my mouth?

triples.relationship: questioning the sufficiency of animal offerings
triples.rationale: Micah asks whether burnt offerings and calves can be the means of taking hold of the Lord. The psalm likewise discusses continual burnt offerings, refuses calves and questions whether God eats bulls' flesh, directing attention beyond merely supplying sacrificial animals.
triples.source_text: With what shall I take hold of the Lord and grasp my God Most High? Shall I take hold of Him with whole burnt offerings, with year-old calves?

target_units.text: I will not rebuke you concerning your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are continually before Me.
I will not receive calves from your house or young goats from your flocks.
For all the forest’s wild animals are Mine, beasts on the mountains and cattle.
I know all the birds of heaven, and the field’s beauty is with Me.
If I become hungry, I will certainly not tell you, for the inhabited world and its fullness are Mine.
Will I eat bulls’ flesh or drink goats’ blood?

triples.relationship: sacrificial abundance contrasted with obedience
triples.rationale: Micah asks whether thousands of rams can satisfy the Lord before stating what He seeks in the next verse. Samuel explicitly places listening and obedience above sacrifice and the fat of rams.
triples.source_text: Will the Lord receive with thousands of rams or with ten thousands of fat-rich torrents? Shall I give my firstborn offspring for impieties, the fruit of my body for the sin of my life?

target_units.text: Samuel said, “Are whole burnt offerings and sacrifices as desirable to the Lord as listening to the Lord’s voice? Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness than the fat of rams.

triples.relationship: firstborn sacrifice considered against the rejection of child offerings
triples.rationale: Micah asks whether a firstborn child could be given for sin, followed by the Lord's ethical requirements. Deuteronomy explicitly rejects the nations' burning of sons and daughters as practices the Lord hates, bearing on the proposed child offering.
triples.source_text: Will the Lord receive with thousands of rams or with ten thousands of fat-rich torrents? Shall I give my firstborn offspring for impieties, the fruit of my body for the sin of my life?

target_units.text: You shall not do so unto the Lord your God; for the abominations which the Lord hated they did unto their gods, for they burn their sons and their daughters with fire unto their gods.

triples.relationship: parallel statement of what the Lord requires
triples.rationale: Micah asks what the Lord seeks and names justice, mercy and readiness to walk with Him. Deuteronomy likewise asks what He requires and names fear, walking in His ways, love, service and keeping His commands.
triples.source_text: Has it been declared to you, O man, what is good? Or what does the Lord seek from you, except to do justice, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?

target_units.text: And now, O Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, but to fear the Lord your God, to walk in all His ways, and to love Him, and to serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul,
to keep the commandments of the Lord your God, and His ordinances which I command you this day, that it may be well with you?

triples.relationship: justice and mercy as weighty requirements
triples.rationale: Micah identifies doing justice and loving mercy among what God seeks. Jesus likewise names justice and mercy among the Law's weightier matters, contrasting their neglect with meticulous tithing.
triples.source_text: Has it been declared to you, O man, what is good? Or what does the Lord seek from you, except to do justice, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?

target_units.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, but have left aside the weightier matters of the Law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness! These you ought to have done without leaving those aside.

triples.relationship: salvation promised to those who fear the Lord
triples.rationale: Micah says the Lord will save those who fear His name. The psalm likewise says He hears and saves those who fear Him, directly joining reverence and rescue.
triples.source_text: The Lord’s voice will be called to the city, and He will save those who fear His name. “Hear, tribe! And who will adorn a city?

target_units.text: He will fulfill the will of those who fear Him; He will hear their plea and save them.

triples.relationship: treasure and the lawless person
triples.rationale: Micah exposes a lawless person's house storing lawless treasures. Proverbs warns that treasures do not profit lawless people and contrasts them with righteousness that rescues from death.
triples.source_text: Is there not fire, and a lawless person’s house storing lawless treasures, and injustice with insolence?

target_units.text: Treasures will not profit lawless people, but righteousness will rescue from death.

triples.relationship: deceptive weights opposed to the legal standard
triples.rationale: Micah questions whether a lawless person can be justified with deceptive weights in a pouch. Deuteronomy expressly forbids differing weights in the pouch, requires just weights and condemns the injustice.
triples.source_text: Will a lawless person be justified with a balance and deceptive weights in a pouch?

target_units.text: You shall not have in your pouch differing weights, a great and a small.
You shall not have in your house differing measures, a great and a small.
You shall have a true and just weight, and you shall have a true and just measure, that your days may be long upon the land which the Lord your God gives you for a possession.
For everyone who does these things, everyone who does injustice, is an abomination unto the Lord your God.

triples.relationship: wealth associated with deceit and impiety
triples.rationale: Micah links accumulated wealth with impiety and the inhabitants' false speech. Jeremiah likewise describes houses filled with deceit whose owners became great and rich, followed by their failure to judge rightly and the promise of visitation.
triples.source_text: From these they filled their wealth with impiety; those inhabiting her spoke falsehoods, and their tongue was exalted in their mouth.

target_units.text: For impious people were found among My people, and they set traps to destroy men and were catching them.
Like a set trap full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit; therefore they became great and rich.
And they transgressed judgment; they did not judge an orphan’s case, and they were not judging a widow’s case.
Shall I not visit for these things? says the Lord. Or will not My soul take vengeance on such a nation?

triples.relationship: punishment for sins preceding agricultural deprivation
triples.rationale: Micah announces striking and obliteration because of sins, followed by hunger and crop losses. Leviticus similarly announces discipline for sins followed by ineffective labor and land and trees failing to yield.
triples.source_text: And I will begin to strike you; I will obliterate you because of your sins.

target_units.text: And if up to this point you do not obey Me, I will discipline you seven times more for your sins.
And I will shatter the arrogance of your pride, and make your heaven iron, and your land as bronze;
and your strength shall be in vain. Your land shall not yield its seed, and the tree of your field shall not yield its fruit.

triples.relationship: shared curse of eating without satisfaction
triples.rationale: Micah says the people will eat but not be filled. Leviticus uses the same eating-without-being-filled warning within the covenant's scarcity-of-bread sanctions.
triples.source_text: You will eat but certainly not be filled. It will grow dark within you and turn aside, and you will certainly not be saved; whoever is saved will be handed over to the sword.

target_units.text: When I afflict you with a scarcity of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in one oven and give back your bread by weight. You shall eat and in no wise be filled.

triples.relationship: parallel loss of grain, wine and olive yield
triples.rationale: Micah announces sowing without reaping, pressing olives without anointing and pressing wine without drinking. Deuteronomy likewise warns of failed grain yield, vineyards whose wine is not drunk and olives that give no oil for anointing.
triples.source_text: You will sow but certainly not reap; you will press olives but certainly not anoint yourself with oil, and you will press wine, but you shall certainly not drink it. The ordinances of My people will be obliterated.

target_units.text: You shall carry much seed into the field, and gather little; for the locust shall devour it.
You shall plant a vineyard and dress it, but shall neither drink wine nor rejoice in it; for the worm shall devour it.
You shall have olive trees throughout all your borders, but shall not anoint yourself with oil; for your olives shall fall away.

triples.relationship: shared imagery of an absent fruit crop
triples.rationale: Micah laments the lack of an available cluster at the vintage. Jeremiah likewise describes vines without grapes and fig trees without figs. Both portray fruitlessness in passages that also address the people's wrongdoing.
triples.source_text: Alas! I have become like someone gathering stubble at harvest and a gleaning at vintage, with no cluster available to eat the first fruits. Alas, my soul,

target_units.text: and they will gather their produce, says the Lord. There is no grape on the vines and no figs on the fig trees, and the leaves have fallen.

triples.relationship: shared lament for vanished faithfulness
triples.rationale: Micah laments that the devout person has perished and no one acts rightly among people. The psalm similarly cries that the holy one is gone and truths have diminished, followed by deceit toward neighbors.
triples.source_text: for the devout person has perished from the earth, and no one acts rightly among people. They all litigate for bloodshed; each crushes his neighbor with crushing.

target_units.text: Save me, Lord, for the holy one is gone; for truths have become few among the sons of men.
Each spoke empty things to his neighbor; deceitful lips spoke with a heart and a heart.

triples.relationship: shared moth-consumption imagery of loss
triples.rationale: Micah pictures removal of the people's good things with a moth eating away. Isaiah likewise speaks of wool eaten by a moth, in contrast to God's lasting righteousness and salvation. The connection is the consuming-moth image; Micah's other wording remains unchanged.
triples.source_text: their good things like a moth eating away and walking upon a measuring rod on the day of watching. Woe, woe! Your punishments have arrived; now they will weep.

target_units.text: Listen to Me, you who know judgment, My people with My law in your heart. Do not fear people’s reproach or be overcome by their contempt.
For a garment will be consumed by time, and wool eaten by a moth. But My righteousness will last for ever, and My salvation through generations of generations.”

triples.relationship: parallel warning against trust in familiar companions
triples.rationale: Micah warns against confidence in friends and even disclosure to a bed companion. Jeremiah likewise warns people to guard against neighbors and not trust brothers because friends act deceitfully.
triples.source_text: Do not put confidence in friends or hope in leaders. With your bed companion, beware of entrusting anything to her.

target_units.text: Each of you, guard against his neighbor, and do not put trust in their brothers, because every brother will trip with the heel, and every friend will walk deceitfully.
Each will mock his friend; they certainly will not speak truth. Their tongue has learned to speak false things; they did wrong and did not cease turning back.

triples.relationship: explicitly corresponding household-division language
triples.rationale: Micah lists son against father, daughter against mother, daughter-in-law against mother-in-law, and enemies within the household. Matthew reproduces the same family divisions and household-enemy statement in Jesus' description of division associated with His coming.
triples.source_text: For a son dishonors his father, a daughter will rise against her mother, a daughter-in-law will rise against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are all the men in his house.

target_units.text: For I came to divide a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law,
and a person’s enemies will be the members of his own household.

triples.relationship: waiting for the Lord and being heard
triples.rationale: The speaker in Micah resolves to wait upon God the Savior and expects Him to listen. The psalm recalls waiting patiently for the Lord and being heard, giving an answered-prayer counterpart to that expectation.
triples.source_text: But I will look toward the Lord; I will wait upon God my Savior. My God will listen to me.

target_units.text: I waited patiently for the Lord; He attended to me and heard my supplication.

triples.relationship: falling, rising and forbidden enemy rejoicing
triples.rationale: The speaker in Micah tells the enemy not to rejoice at the speaker's fall because rising will follow. Proverbs likewise says the righteous fall and rise and then forbids rejoicing over an enemy's fall.
triples.source_text: Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen! I will rise, for if I sit in darkness, the Lord will shine for me.

target_units.text: for the righteous will fall seven times and rise, but the impious will grow weak amid evils.

for the Lord will see, and it will not please Him, and He will turn His wrath away from him.

triples.relationship: acknowledgment of sin amid divine displeasure
triples.rationale: The speaker in Micah bears the Lord's anger because of acknowledged sin, while awaiting vindication. Lamentations similarly questions grumbling over one's sin, calls for return to the Lord and acknowledges godlessness and unappeased divine displeasure.
triples.source_text: I will bear the Lord’s anger, for I sinned against Him, until He vindicates my case. He will execute my judgment and bring me out into the light; I will see His righteousness.

target_units.text: Why should a living person grumble, a man concerning his sin?

triples.relationship: shared taunt about God's whereabouts
triples.rationale: Micah records an enemy asking where the speaker's God is. The psalmist likewise hears the repeated taunt, Where is your God, while suffering in tears. Both place that question in the mouth of those aggravating the afflicted person's distress.
triples.source_text: My enemy will see and clothe herself in shame, she who says to me, “Where is the Lord your God?” My eyes will look upon her; now she will become a trampling place like mud in the streets

target_units.text: My tears became my bread day and night, while it is said to me every day, “Where is your God?”

triples.relationship: judgment according to the fruits of conduct
triples.rationale: Micah attributes the land's obliteration to the fruits of its inhabitants' practices. Jeremiah states that the Lord gives to each according to their ways and the fruits of their practices, articulating the principle behind such recompense.
triples.source_text: The land will become an obliteration together with those inhabiting it, from the fruits of their practices.

target_units.text: I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices.

triples.relationship: prayer to Israel's divine shepherd
triples.rationale: Micah asks God to shepherd the people, described as the sheep of His inheritance. The psalm likewise addresses the One shepherding Israel and guiding Joseph like sheep, then asks Him to come and save.
triples.source_text: Shepherd Thy people with Thy rod, the sheep of Thine inheritance, camping by themselves in a forest amid Carmel. They will graze in Bashan and Gilead as in the days of old.

target_units.text: Thou who shepherdest Israel, pay attention, Thou who guidest Joseph like sheep; Thou who sittest upon the cherubim, appear.
Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh, rouse Thy dominion, and come to save us.
God, turn us back; make Thy face shine, and we shall be saved.

triples.relationship: explicit recollection of the exodus as a pattern of wonders
triples.rationale: Micah promises wonders like those seen at the departure from Egypt. Exodus narrates the Lord rescuing Israel from the Egyptians and Israel seeing His great hand, providing the recalled deliverance pattern.
triples.source_text: And as in the days of your departure from Egypt, you will see wonderful things.

target_units.text: The Lord rescued Israel that day from the Egyptians’ hand, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.
Israel saw the great hand in what the Lord had done to the Egyptians. The people feared the Lord and trusted God and His attendant Moses.

triples.relationship: nations seeing and mouths falling silent
triples.rationale: Micah depicts nations seeing God's work and putting hands over their mouths. Isaiah likewise depicts nations marveling and kings closing their mouths as they see what had not been proclaimed to them. Both portray a silenced response to what they witness, in differing prophetic settings.
triples.source_text: Nations will see and be ashamed of all their strength. They will place hands over their mouth; their ears will be deafened.

target_units.text: so many nations will marvel at him, and kings will close their mouths. For those to whom he was not proclaimed will see, and those who have not heard will understand.

triples.relationship: shared serpent-and-earth humiliation imagery
triples.rationale: Micah compares the nations licking dust with snakes moving along the ground. Genesis condemns the serpent to go on breast and belly and eat earth. The connection is the degrading serpent-and-earth image, not an identification of the nations with that individual serpent.
triples.source_text: They will lick dust like snakes dragging along the earth; they will be thrown into turmoil in their confinement. They will be astonished at the Lord our God and fear Thee.

target_units.text: And the Lord God said to the serpent: Because you have done this, cursed are you above all cattle and all the wild beasts of the earth. Upon your breast and belly you shall go, and earth you shall eat all the days of your life.

triples.relationship: shared dust-licking image of humbled opponents
triples.rationale: Micah depicts the nations licking dust and fearing God. The royal psalm likewise describes enemies licking dust, with kings bowing and nations serving, using the same action to express humbled opposition.

triples.relationship: shared question of God's incomparability
triples.rationale: Micah asks who is a God like the Lord in the context of mercy and forgiveness. The exodus song similarly asks who is like the Lord among the gods, praising His wondrous works. The shared rhetorical question introduces praise with different immediate emphases.
triples.source_text: Who is a God like Thee, removing injustices and passing over impieties for the remaining ones of His inheritance? He did not retain His anger as a testimony, because He desires mercy.

target_units.text: Who is like Thee among the gods, O Lord? Who is like Thee, glorified among the holy ones, marvellous in glories, working wonders?

triples.relationship: shared mercy and removal of wrongdoing
triples.rationale: Micah praises God for removing injustices, passing over impieties and desiring mercy. Exodus's proclamation of His name likewise emphasizes mercy and the taking away of lawlessness, injustice and sins.
triples.source_text: Who is a God like Thee, removing injustices and passing over impieties for the remaining ones of His inheritance? He did not retain His anger as a testimony, because He desires mercy.

target_units.text: The Lord passed before him and proclaimed, “The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, slow to anger, abundant in mercy and true,

preserving righteousness and showing mercy to thousands, taking away lawlessness, injustice, and sins, yet not cleansing the guilty, bringing the fathers’ lawlessness upon children and children’s children to the third and fourth generation.”

triples.relationship: spatial imagery of sins removed from the people
triples.rationale: Micah pictures injustices sunk and sins thrown into the sea's depths. The psalm describes lawless deeds removed as far as east from west. Both use distance or depth to portray God's removal of the people's wrongdoing.
triples.source_text: He Himself will turn back and pity us; He will sink our injustices, and they will be thrown into the depths of the sea—all our sins.

target_units.text: As far as the east is distant from the west, He removed our lawless deeds from us.

triples.relationship: appeal to the oath given to Abraham
triples.rationale: Micah anticipates mercy to Abraham according to what God swore to the fathers. Genesis records the Lord swearing by Himself to bless Abraham's offspring and, through that offspring, the nations.
triples.source_text: Thou wilt grant truth to Jacob, mercy to Abraham, just as Thou didst swear to our fathers in the former days.
